title: The merciful (Matthew 5:7)

cards: A car cuts in front of another. In seconds, a whole biography gets written for the other driver: selfish, entitled, probably always like this. Now flip it.

When you're the one cutting in, the story changes: late, a confusing lane, didn't see them. Mercy for yourself comes easily; for everyone else it gets rusty. Some readers notice a turn in the sermon here.
The first four beatitudes describe people in need: empty hands, grief, meekness, hunger. The next ones describe what people give. And the first thing given is mercy.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Blessed are the merciful: for they shall obtain mercy." The Greek word for mercy is eleos. If you've ever heard a church sing Kyrie eleison, that's the same word: Lord, have mercy.
In the Bible, mercy is something you do with your hands, not only something you feel. In the story of the Good Samaritan, the neighbor is the one who showed mercy: he stopped, and bandaged.
Behind it is a rich Hebrew world.
One Hebrew word, chesed, means steady, loyal love that doesn't quit. Another, rachamim, shares its root with the Hebrew word for womb: the love a mother feels for the child she carried.
Not a judge grudgingly letting you off. A mother's gut.
The prophet Micah summed up what God asks: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God."
Now the promise: they shall obtain mercy. It isn't a trade, as if you could buy God's mercy with your own. Christian teachers say God's mercy comes first.

But there's a loop in it. Later, Jesus tells a story about a servant forgiven a huge debt who throws a fellow servant in prison over a small one. When the master hears, he hands the unforgiving servant back to his debt.
Christians read it this way: mercy isn't earned, but mercy received is meant to flow on, and a heart that refuses to give it closes itself to receiving it.

how: Kyrie eleison, Lord have mercy, is sung or said in Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran worship, and Catholic and other Christians practice the works of mercy: feeding the hungry, visiting the sick and prisoners, and forgiving wrongs.

games.q: in Jesus's story, a servant is forgiven a huge debt. then a fellow servant owes him a little. what does he do?
games.why: he throws him in prison, and his master is furious. mercy received is meant to flow on.

practice: Think of someone you've judged recently, a coworker, a relative, a stranger, a public figure, and write in your mind the generous version of their story, the one you'd write for yourself: maybe they're exhausted, maybe scared, maybe they didn't see.
You don't have to excuse anything; just let their story be as complicated as yours. If you pray, you can pray the old words, Lord, have mercy, for them and for you.

wordCard.voice: Mercy. Eleos in Greek, as in Kyrie eleison; in Hebrew, loyal love and a mother's tenderness. The fifth beatitude.

orig.note: Greek: the merciful. from eleos, mercy, as in Kyrie eleison.
